concepts.name: Electric charge: two types, positive and negative
concepts.why: The effects of static electricity are explained by a physical quantity not previously introduced, called electric charge. There are only two types of charge, one called positive and the other called negative, and we know there are two because rubbing certain materials together in controlled ways always produces one type on one material and the opposite type on the other. Glass rubbed with silk becomes positive and the silk negative, and the names are a convention that goes back to Franklin.
concepts.evidence: The section opens with the four basic characteristics of static electricity, Figure 18.4 shows the glass rod and the silk exploring the force between charges, and the AP items on the rubbed rod and on the objects W, X, Y and Z test the two types directly.

concepts.name: Like charges repel, unlike charges attract, and the force decreases with distance
concepts.why: Two glass rods rubbed with silk repel one another, since each carries positive charge, and two silk cloths so rubbed repel too, while the rod and the silk attract because their charges are opposite. The force between charges decreases with distance. These two facts are the whole of what is needed to explain static cling, the balloon on the wall and the hair that stands on end, and Coulomb’s law will later say exactly how the force depends on the charges and their separation.
concepts.evidence: The second and third characteristics of static electricity state it, Figure 18.4 draws the three cases, the Van de Graaff photograph of Figure 18.6 shows hair repelled strand from strand, and the AP items on attracting and repelling objects and on the comb and the paper test it.

concepts.name: Electrons and protons carry the charge of ordinary matter
concepts.why: Normal matter is made of atoms, and atoms contain positive and negative charges, usually in equal amounts. In the planetary model, negative electrons orbit a much heavier positive nucleus whose charge is due to its protons; the neutron carries no charge. Nearly all charge in nature is due to electrons and protons, whose charges are identical in magnitude but opposite in sign, and the other charged particles seen in cosmic rays and accelerators survive only a short time.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.5 draws the planetary model, the Things Great and Small box states that all charge is carried by electrons and protons, and Figure 18.6 shows the charges in a single hair; the AP item on which particle is removed when a rod is rubbed against silk turns on electrons being the mobile charge.

concepts.name: The elementary charge, $|\kqe| = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$
concepts.why: All charged objects in nature are integral multiples of one basic quantity of charge, the magnitude of the charge on a single electron or proton, $|q_\text{e}| = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ C. The symbol $q$ is commonly used for charge and the subscript e indicates the charge of a single electron or proton. There is no directly observed charge smaller than this; the quarks inside a proton are believed to carry $-\tfrac13$ and $+\tfrac23$ of it, but they have never been seen alone.
concepts.evidence: The section states the value as its first equation, the SI unit is defined by counting protons to make one coulomb, Figure 18.7 draws the fractional quark charges adding to one $q_\text{e}$, and the problems on the charge of a lightning bolt in fundamental units and on the electrons in a nanocoulomb depend on it.

concepts.name: Count the electrons or protons that make up a charge
concepts.why: The SI unit of charge is the coulomb, and the number of protons needed to make 1.00 C is $6.25 \times 10^{18}$, one coulomb divided by the charge on one proton; the same number of electrons carries $-1.00$ C. Any charge, then, is turned into a count of electrons by dividing by $|q_\text{e}|$, and a count of electrons moved through a wire or removed from a neutral object is turned back into coulombs by multiplying.
concepts.evidence: The section works the protons per coulomb as its second equation, and every problem of the section, the electrons in −2.00 nC, the coulombs moved through a calculator and through a starter motor, the fundamental units of charge in a 40.0 C lightning bolt, is this division or multiplication.

concepts.name: Rubbing separates existing charge
concepts.why: Charges in atoms and molecules can be separated by rubbing materials together, because some atoms and molecules have a greater affinity for electrons than others and become negatively charged by close contact, leaving the other material positively charged. Batteries separate charge by chemical interactions instead. No charge is created or destroyed when charges are separated in this way; existing charges are moved about, and for macroscopic objects negatively charged means an excess of electrons and positively charged a depletion of them.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.8 draws the amber and the cloth before, during and after rubbing with the counts of the two charges equal at every stage, Figure 18.3’s amber and silk are the ancient case, and the AP items on two neutral objects rubbed together and on the charged object gaining electrons from a neutral one test the accounting.

concepts.name: The law of conservation of charge
concepts.why: Total charge is constant in any process. Rubbing only moves existing charge about, and even in the exotic situations of a particle accelerator, where mass is created from energy in the amount $\Delta m = E/c^2$, a charged particle is always created together with another of opposite charge, so that the total charge created is zero, and when a particle and its antimatter counterpart annihilate the total charge is zero before and after. The law is absolute and has never been observed to be violated, which puts charge on the short list of quantities, with energy, momentum and angular momentum, that nature always conserves.
concepts.evidence: The boxed law is the section’s central statement, Figure 18.9 draws an electron–positron pair created and then annihilated with $q_\text{tot} = 0$ throughout, the Making Connections box sets charge beside the other conserved quantities, and the AP items on the three colliding latex spheres and on the charge left on the two objects after a transfer apply it.

concepts.name: Conductor
concepts.why: Some substances, such as metals and salty water, allow charges to move through them with relative ease. Some of the electrons in metals are not bound to individual atoms, and these free electrons can move through the material much as air moves through loose sand; salty water and similar materials contain free ions instead, an ion being an atom or molecule with a nonzero total charge. Any substance that has free electrons or free ions and allows charge to move relatively freely through it is a conductor.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the conductor in its first paragraph, Figure 18.10’s power adapter is the everyday case, the electroscope of Figure 18.11 works because its stem and leaves conduct, and the AP item asking whether a sphere charged by induction must be a conductor tests the definition.

concepts.name: Insulator
concepts.why: Other substances, such as glass, do not allow charges to move through them; these are insulators. Electrons and ions in insulators are bound in the structure and cannot move easily, as much as $10^{23}$ times more slowly than in conductors. Pure water and dry table salt are insulators, whereas molten salt and salty water are conductors, and the rubber and plastic round a wire keep its charge from escaping outward.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the insulator against the conductor, the glass rod of Figure 18.11 must touch the electroscope because it is an insulator, and the conceptual question on the polished car and the AP item on the sphere charged by induction turn on which materials let charge move.

concepts.name: Charging by contact
concepts.why: An object can be charged by touching it with a charged object, and it obtains the same sign of charge. When a positively charged glass rod touches the ball of an electroscope, electrons are attracted to the top of the electroscope and some are transferred to the rod, leaving the electroscope with a net positive charge whose repulsion in the light gold leaves separates them; the rod loses some of its excess charge in the transfer. Because the rod is an insulator, it must actually touch the electroscope to transfer charge.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.11 draws the electroscope charged by contact in three panels, the passage explains the electrons’ motion, and the AP items on giving a sphere the same sign of charge as a pie plate and on the two experiments with a glass rod and an electroscope test it against induction.

concepts.name: Polarization
concepts.why: Polarization is the separation of charges in an object that remains neutral. When a charged rod is brought near a neutral conductor, charge of the opposite sign is attracted to the near side and like charge is left on the far side; in an insulator the distribution of charge in each atom or molecule is shifted slightly, and some molecules, like water, are polar, with a natural separation of charge although they are neutral overall.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.12(b), 18.13(a) and 18.14 all draw it, the passage on charging by induction names it, and the keyed AP item on the balloon brought near the sphere asks for the phenomenon by name.

concepts.name: Grounding
concepts.why: A conductor is grounded when a conducting wire is run from it to the ground. Since the earth is large and most ground is a good conductor, it can supply or accept excess charge easily, so a grounded conductor loses any excess charge to the earth or draws from it whatever a nearby charge attracts. Breaking the ground connection before a nearby charged object is removed leaves the conductor with a net charge.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.13(b) and (c) draw the ground wire attached and then broken, the summary defines grounding as the transfer of charge to and from the earth’s large reservoir, and the conceptual question asking what grounding is and what it does to a charged conductor and a charged insulator tests it.

concepts.name: Charging by induction
concepts.why: It is not necessary to transfer excess charge directly to an object in order to charge it. A charged rod brought near two touching neutral spheres attracts opposite charge to the near sphere and leaves the other with like charge, and if the spheres are separated before the rod is pulled away each keeps a net charge. A single sphere can be charged the same way by grounding it while the rod is near, then breaking the ground connection. The object charged by induction receives the opposite charge to the rod, and the rod loses none of its excess charge, so the process can be repeated.
concepts.evidence: Figures 18.12 and 18.13 draw the two methods in four panels each, the passage says twice that the induced charge is opposite and the rod is not depleted, and six of the section’s nine AP items, from the balloon near the sphere through the two suspended metal balls, walk the reader through induction step by step.

concepts.name: A charged object attracts a neutral one
concepts.why: Neutral objects can be attracted to any charged object, whether its charge is positive or negative. When a charged rod is brought near a neutral substance, opposite charge is attracted nearer the rod while like charge is repelled, and since the electrostatic force decreases with distance, the repulsion of the like charges, which are farther away, is weaker than the attraction of the unlike charges, which are nearer, so there is a net attraction. That is why polished amber picks up straw, a comb picks up paper, and a charged rod bends a stream of water.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.14 draws the polarized insulator and conductor with the net attraction, the Check Your Understanding box asks why the water in Figure 18.15 bends toward the rod, and the conceptual questions on dust attracted to both the rod and the silk and on the freshly polished car turn on it.

concepts.name: Coulomb’s law, $\kF = k|\kqone \kqtwo|/r^2$
concepts.why: The main features of the electrostatic force, two types of charge, like charges repelling and unlike attracting, and the decrease of the force with distance, were refined in the late eighteenth century into a mathematical formula named for Charles Coulomb. Coulomb’s law gives the magnitude of the force between two point charges separated by a distance $r$: it is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. Modern experiments have verified the inverse square to one part in $10^{16}$, and no exception has ever been found, even within the atom.
concepts.evidence: The boxed law is the section’s statement, Figure 18.17 draws the force on each charge for like and unlike pairs, Example 18.1 evaluates it for the electron and proton of a hydrogen atom, and every problem of the section, from the two pith balls to the two charges 3.00 m apart, is the law solved for one of its four quantities.

concepts.name: Coulomb’s constant, $k = 8.99 \times 10^{9}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$
concepts.why: In SI units the constant in Coulomb’s law is $k = 8.988 \times 10^{9}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$, usually rounded to $8.99 \times 10^{9}$. Its size is what makes a coulomb such a large amount of charge: two charges of 1 C each, held 1 m apart, would push on one another with a force of nearly $10^{10}$ N, which is why the charges of everyday static electricity are nanocoulombs and microcoulombs.
concepts.evidence: The constant is stated in the boxed law and used in every worked substitution of the section; the AP item on two charges of 1 C separated by 0.5 m and the problem on two 1 C charges a kilometer apart show how large the force still is.

concepts.name: The Coulomb force acts along the line joining the charges, and Newton’s third law applies
concepts.why: The electrostatic force is a vector quantity expressed in newtons, and it is understood to be along the line joining the two charges, repulsive for like charges and attractive for unlike. Newton’s third law applies as usual: the force on $q_1$ is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force $q_1$ exerts on $q_2$, whatever the sizes of the two charges.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.17 draws the pair of forces for like and for unlike charges with arrows of the same length, the boxed law says the force is along the joining line, and the problem on the test charge halfway between two positive charges asks for the direction of the force.

concepts.name: Scale the Coulomb force when a charge or the separation changes
concepts.why: Because the force is proportional to each charge and inversely proportional to the square of the separation, a change in any one of them changes the force by a factor that can be read off without evaluating the constant. Halving the distance multiplies the force by four, tripling it divides by nine, doubling one charge doubles the force, and a change of the force by a factor of 10 needs a change of the distance by $\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2$ either way.
concepts.evidence: The three AP items introduced by ‘suppose that the electrostatic force between two charges is F’ are this skill, as are the problems on a force of 5.00 N when the distance is tripled, on the separation that raises the force by a factor of 25, and on the factor of 3.2 that changes the force by a factor of 10.

concepts.name: The Coulomb force is far stronger than gravity between particles, but it can cancel
concepts.why: For an electron and a proton the ratio of the electrostatic force to the gravitational force is $2.27 \times 10^{39}$, at any separation, since both fall off as the inverse square and the distance cancels in the ratio. Gravity is therefore completely negligible where individual charged particles interact. On a large scale the reverse is true: most objects are nearly electrically neutral, so the attractive and repulsive Coulomb forces nearly cancel, while gravity, which is always attractive, adds up and dominates between large objects.
concepts.evidence: Example 18.1 computes both forces at the hydrogen atom’s separation and takes the ratio, the Arp 87 photograph of Figure 18.16 sets the galaxies against the atom, the summary states the contrast, and the AP item and the problem on the ratio for two electrons and for two protons repeat the calculation.

concepts.name: The Coulomb force field depends on the test charge
concepts.why: A field is a way of conceptualizing and mapping the force that surrounds any object and acts on another object at a distance without apparent physical connection, as the gravitational field of the earth maps the force a mass would feel at any point. The Coulomb force field surrounding a charge $Q$ extends throughout space, and Coulomb’s law gives its magnitude as $F = k|qQ|/r^2$ on a test charge $q$; but both its magnitude and its direction depend on the test charge as well as on $Q$, so it is not unique at any point in space.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.18 draws the force of one charge $Q$ on two different test charges at the same distance, one repelled and one attracted more strongly, and the conceptual question asking whether the Coulomb force is unique at a point in space tests the idea against the electric field.

concepts.name: Point charge and test charge
concepts.why: The charge that creates a field is a point charge, written $Q$, and the charge set down in the field to feel it is a test charge, written $q$. The test charge is taken to be positive, so that the field has the direction of the force on it, and so small that it does not alter the charge distribution creating the field.
concepts.evidence: The passage defines both in introducing the Coulomb force field, the glossary carries both terms, and the conceptual question asking why the test charge must be vanishingly small tests the second condition.

concepts.name: The electric field, $\kEf = \kF/\kq$
concepts.why: To have a field that depends only on the charge creating it, the electric field is defined as the ratio of the Coulomb force to the positive test charge it acts on. So defined, it represents only the charge creating it and is unique at every point in space, its direction is the direction of the force on a positive test charge, and its units are newtons per coulomb. It is a vector, and fields due to several charges add like vectors.
concepts.evidence: The definition is the section’s first equation and is repeated in the summary, Example 18.2 computes the field of a point charge and Example 18.3 uses the definition to get a force from it, and the AP item on the direction of the field of a negative charge and the problems on the field that exerts a given force on a given charge apply it.

concepts.name: The force on a charge in a field, $\kF = \kq\kEf$
concepts.why: If the electric field is known, the electrostatic force on any charge $q$ is obtained by multiplying the charge by the field. The force on a positive charge is in the direction of the field, and the force on a negative charge is opposite to it, which is what a negative sign on $q$ says.
concepts.evidence: Example 18.3 finds the 0.180 N attractive force of a $7.20 \times 10^{5}$ N/C field on a −0.250 μC charge and remarks that the force is opposite to the field because the charge is negative; the keyed problem on a 3.50 μC charge in a 250 N/C field and the problems on the field that exerts a westward force on an electron and the force the same field exerts on a proton repeat it.

concepts.name: The field of a point charge, $\kEf = k|\kQch|/r^2$
concepts.why: Applying the definition of the field to Coulomb’s force on a test charge, the test charge cancels and the magnitude of the electric field of a point charge is $E = k|Q|/r^2$. The field depends only on the charge $Q$ and the distance $r$ from it, and is completely independent of the test charge; it points away from a positive $Q$ and toward a negative one.
concepts.evidence: The derivation and the result are the section’s middle equations, Example 18.2 evaluates it for 2.00 nC at 5.00 mm, and the problems on the field 2.00 m from a 5.00 mC Van de Graaff terminal and on the point charge that creates 10,000 N/C at 0.250 m turn it around.

concepts.name: The direction of the electric field
concepts.why: Because the field is defined for a positive test charge, it points away from a positive charge and toward a negative charge, and the force on a charge placed in it is along the field for a positive charge and against it for a negative one. A field found to be positive in a calculation is a field pointing away from the charge that creates it.
concepts.evidence: Example 18.2’s discussion reads the sign of its result as a direction, Example 18.3 reverses the direction for a negative charge, and the AP items on the inward field of a negative charge and on the sign of a particle pushed inward by a positive one test it.

concepts.name: Electric field lines
concepts.why: Since the electric field has both magnitude and direction, it is a vector, and it can be drawn at any point as an arrow whose length is its magnitude. In the standard representation the arrows are replaced by continuous field lines having the same direction at any point as the field, and the closeness of the lines is directly related to the strength of the field. Field lines are a map of infinitesimal force vectors, a pictorial tool and not a physical entity, and the same representation is used for gravitational, magnetic and other fields.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.19 draws the field of a positive charge first as arrows and then as lines, Figure 18.20 draws a positive, an equal negative and a larger negative charge, and the problems asking the reader to sketch the lines near $+q$ and near $-3.00q$ test the representation.

concepts.name: The five properties of electric field lines
concepts.why: For any charge distribution, field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative charges, or at infinity for an isolated charge; the number of lines leaving a positive charge or entering a negative one is proportional to the magnitude of the charge; the strength of the field is proportional to the number of lines per unit area perpendicular to them, which is why the field of a point charge, falling as $1/r^2$, is exactly represented by lines spreading over an area that grows as $r^2$; the direction of the field is tangent to the line at any point; and field lines can never cross, since the field is unique at every point and a crossing would give it two directions.
concepts.evidence: The five properties are listed in the passage and again in the summary, the AP item on the three charged objects R, S and T asks the reader to read signs and magnitudes off a field diagram, the conceptual question on the three regions I, II and III asks where the field is strongest, weakest and most uniform, and the problem on the ratio of two charges from their field lines uses the second property.

concepts.name: The total field of several charges is the vector sum of their fields
concepts.why: In many situations there are multiple charges, and the total electric field they create at a point is the vector sum of the individual fields created by each charge. The field of each charge at the point is found from $E = k|Q|/r^2$ with the direction of the force on a positive test charge there, and the fields are then added with the same vector techniques used for forces and velocities.
concepts.evidence: The passage states it before Example 18.4, the summary says fields due to multiple charges add like vectors, and the AP items on the square of four charges and on the field along the axis of the three objects R, S and T rest on it.

concepts.name: Add the fields of two charges at a point
concepts.why: To find the total field at a point, find the field of each charge there in magnitude and direction, pretending a positive test charge sits at the point to fix the directions, then add the vectors. When the two fields are perpendicular, as in Example 18.4, the Pythagorean theorem gives the magnitude and the inverse tangent gives the direction; otherwise components or graphical techniques are used.
concepts.evidence: Example 18.4 adds the $1.124 \times 10^{5}$ N/C field of $q_1$ and the $0.5619 \times 10^{5}$ N/C field of $q_2$ at the origin to $1.26 \times 10^{5}$ N/C at $63.4°$, with Figure 18.21 drawing the two arrows and their resultant; 18.7’s problems on the field at the center of a square and of a triangle of charges repeat the method.

concepts.name: Find the total force on a charge from several charges
concepts.why: The total force on a charge is the vector sum of the Coulomb forces the other charges exert on it, each along the line joining the pair and each found from Coulomb’s law; equivalently, it is the charge multiplied by the total electric field at its position. Symmetry often settles the direction before any number is entered, and a point where the net force is zero is where the individual forces cancel.
concepts.evidence: The section’s first objective is to calculate the total force exerted on a test charge from more than one charge, the AP items on the dipole and the third charge and on the square of four charges ask for net forces, and 18.3’s problem on where a third charge feels no net force and 18.7’s problems on the force on the charge at the center of a square rest on it.

concepts.name: The field of two like charges and of two unlike charges
concepts.why: The field of two point charges can be drawn by finding the total field at representative points and drawing lines consistent with them. Between two like charges the field is weaker, the lines farther apart, because the fields of the two charges oppose one another there, and at a great distance the field becomes that of a single larger charge. Between two unlike charges the field is stronger, since the two fields point the same way, and at large distances it is weak, since the two fields subtract, looking like the field of a smaller single charge.
concepts.evidence: Figures 18.22 and 18.23 draw the two positive charges, the two negative charges and the positive–negative pair, the passage explains each pattern, and the problems asking the reader to sketch the lines a long distance from each distribution and near two opposite charges of unequal size test it.

concepts.name: Sketch the field lines of a charge distribution
concepts.why: A field-line drawing is built from the five properties: lines leave positive charges and enter negative ones in numbers proportional to the charges, they never cross, their direction is the field’s and their closeness is its strength. Near a single charge the lines are radial, near two charges they bend as Figures 18.22 and 18.23 show, and far from any distribution they look like the lines of one charge equal to the total.
concepts.evidence: Four problems of the section ask for a sketch, near $+q$ and $-3.00q$, far from the distributions of Figure 18.23, near two unequal opposite charges, and 18.7’s problems ask for sketches near conductors and a charged insulating rod.

concepts.name: Large biological molecules are charged
concepts.why: Classical electrostatics has an important role in molecular biology, because the large molecules so important to life, proteins and nucleic acids, are usually electrically charged. DNA carries about two fundamental charges per 0.3 nm along its length, and it is the electrostatic force that holds the molecule together and gives it its structure and strength; since the Coulomb force falls as $1/r^2$, the base pairs must be close enough, about 0.3 nm within a base and 1 nm between the strands, for the force to hold them.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.24 shows the double helix, the passage gives the charge per length and the two distances, and the section’s summary states that many molecules in living organisms, such as DNA, carry a charge.

concepts.name: Polar molecules and dipoles
concepts.why: Water is a strongly polar molecule: its ten electrons tend to remain closer to the oxygen nucleus than to the hydrogen nuclei, which creates two centers of equal and opposite charge, a dipole, whose magnitude is the dipole moment. The oxygen side is slightly negative and the hydrogen ends slightly positive, and the attraction of opposite charges between molecules follows. A molecule with a natural separation of charge is more strongly affected by other charges than one with a uniform distribution.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.25 draws two water molecules with their δ⁻ and δ⁺ ends attracting, the passage under Polarity of Water Molecules defines the dipole, and 18.2’s Check Your Understanding on the bent stream of water and 18.3’s conceptual questions on humidity and on the water molecule of its figure are answered by it.

concepts.name: Screening of the Coulomb force in cells
concepts.why: Electrostatic forces do not play a larger role in biology than they do, in spite of so many charged molecules, because the force is diluted by screening: the two centers of charge in a water molecule, and the Na⁺, K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions inside and outside cells, terminate some of the field lines coming from a free charge, reducing the strength of the Coulomb interaction. One might say that screening makes the Coulomb force a short-range force rather than a long-range one; microtubules within a cell seem to extend electric fields over larger distances in spite of it.
concepts.evidence: The passage introduces screening after the DNA discussion and explains it through the water dipole and the cell’s ions, the summary states that a Coulomb field may be reduced or blocked by other nearby charges, and the conceptual question on the charged cell membrane asks where its field is and is not.

concepts.name: Electrostatic equilibrium
concepts.why: Conductors contain free charges that move easily, and when excess charge is placed on a conductor or the conductor is put into a static electric field, the charges quickly respond to reach a steady state called electrostatic equilibrium. The free charges move until there is no force left to move them, which is the condition every property of a conductor in equilibrium follows from. In metals the free charges are electrons, but the motion of a positive charge one way is equivalent to a negative charge moving the other.
concepts.evidence: The section opens by defining the state, Figure 18.26 draws a free charge driven to the surface until the parallel force is zero, and the boxed Properties of a Conductor in Electrostatic Equilibrium list what follows.

concepts.name: At the surface of a conductor in equilibrium, the field is perpendicular to the surface
concepts.why: There can be no component of the field parallel to the surface of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, since if there were it would exert a force $F_\parallel = qE_\parallel$ on the free charges and produce further movement of charge. The free charges move until the field is perpendicular to the surface, so just outside a conductor the field lines are perpendicular to it, ending or beginning on charges on the surface.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.26 resolves an applied field into its parallel and perpendicular components and shows the charge moving until the parallel one is gone, the second boxed property states the result, and the conceptual questions on whether the object of the figure with lines passing through it is a conductor, and whether perpendicular lines would prove it one, test it.

concepts.name: The electric field is zero inside a conductor
concepts.why: A conductor placed in an electric field is polarized: its free charges move until the field lines end on excess negative charge on one part of the surface and begin again on excess positive charge on the opposite side, and no field is left inside, since free charges would continue moving in response to any field until it was neutralized. The field outside becomes stronger near the conductor and disappears entirely within it.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.27 draws a neutral sphere in an originally uniform field with the lines bending to meet it at right angles and none inside, the Misconception Alert makes the point for a charged sphere, the first boxed property states it, and the Faraday cage of the applications rests on it.

concepts.name: Excess charge resides on the surface, and a charged sphere’s field is that of a point charge
concepts.why: Excess charges placed on a spherical conductor repel one another and move until they are evenly distributed on its surface, forced there until the field inside is zero; any excess charge resides entirely on the surface or surfaces of a conductor. Outside a charged sphere the field is exactly the same as if the conductor were replaced by a point charge at its center equal to the excess charge.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.28 draws the uniformly charged sphere with its radial field, the Misconception Alert and the third boxed property state it, the keyed AP item on where the field of a charged sphere is weakest and the one on the field at three times the distance with the charge doubled apply the point-charge equivalence, and 18.8’s Van de Graaff and Earth’s-charge problems use it.

concepts.name: Two parallel plates with opposite charges make a uniform field
concepts.why: A very uniform electric field is created by two metal plates with equal and opposite excess charges. The properties of conductors in equilibrium make the charges distribute themselves uniformly except near the edges, producing field lines that are uniformly spaced, hence uniform in strength, and perpendicular to the flat surfaces, hence uniform in direction; the edge effects matter less when the plates are close together. Such a field gives charges a uniform acceleration, as in the electron gun of an old cathode-ray tube.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.29 draws the plates and their field, the AP item on where the field between two plates is strongest and the conceptual question on what close means for the plate separation test it, and 18.8’s problems on the electron accelerated between plates, deflected between plates and the Millikan oil drop use the uniform field.

concepts.name: Earth’s electric field
concepts.why: A near-uniform electric field of about 150 N/C, directed downward, surrounds Earth, maintained in fair weather between the positive ionosphere, a layer of charged particles about 100 km up, and the largely negative Earth, both of which are conductors. In storm conditions clouds form and local fields can be larger and reversed; if the field exceeds about $3 \times 10^{6}$ N/C the insulating air breaks down and becomes conducting, and the discharge is lightning or corona.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.30 shows the fair-weather field and a storm in two photographs, the passage under Earth’s Electric Field gives the numbers, and 18.8’s problem on the excess charge that produces 150 N/C at the surface and its problem on the practical limit of a field in air use them.

concepts.name: Excess charge concentrates at the sharpest points of a conductor
concepts.why: On a nonuniform conductor the excess charges become concentrated at the sharpest points. The forces between identical pairs of charges at either end of the conductor are the same, but only the component parallel to the surface moves charge apart, and that component is greatest on the flattest surface and smallest at the most pointed end, so the charges are left closer together there and the field, which must meet the surface at right angles, is strongest there. An external field polarizes a conductor the same way, with its most concentrated charge at its most pointed end.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.31 draws the pair of forces at the two ends, the resulting field, and an uncharged conductor polarized in a uniform field; Figure 18.32 draws the very pointed conductor whose field is strong enough to remove charge; and the problems asking for the field near an oblong conductor and a nonuniformly charged rod test it.

concepts.name: Lightning rods and smooth conductors
concepts.why: On a very sharply curved surface the charges are so concentrated that the field can be great enough to remove them from the surface. Lightning rods work best when they are most pointed, because the charge a storm cloud induces on a building is bled away continually through the point, preventing the more dramatic strike. When the transfer of charge is to be prevented instead, as on a high-voltage transmission line or the terminal of a Van de Graaff generator, the conductor is made very smooth with as large a radius of curvature as possible.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.33 sets a pointed lightning rod beside the smooth sphere of a Van de Graaff, the passage under Applications of Conductors explains both, and the conceptual questions on the sign of charge a point removes, on the golfer with a metal club, and on grounding a lightning rod against merely attaching it test the idea.

concepts.name: The Faraday cage
concepts.why: A Faraday cage is a metal shield that encloses a volume: all electrical charges reside on its outside surface and there is no electric field inside, so it keeps stray fields in the environment from interfering with sensitive measurements such as the signals inside a nerve cell. A car’s metal body is a Faraday cage, which is why it is best to stay inside it during an electrical storm or if a live wire has fallen on it, provided you remain totally inside.
concepts.evidence: The passage under Applications of Conductors defines the cage and gives the car as the case, the summary restates it, and the conceptual questions on being safe from lightning inside an automobile and on the person carrying an excess charge apply it.

concepts.name: The Van de Graaff generator
concepts.why: A Van de Graaff generator uses both smooth and pointed surfaces, and conductors and insulators, to build large static charges and hence large voltages. A pointed conductor sprays charge onto a moving insulating belt near the bottom, a second pointed conductor inside the large sphere picks it off at the top, and the charge moves to the sphere’s outside surface, so a very large excess charge can be deposited before the field polarizes and ionizes the surrounding material and lets it escape. The first was built in 1931 for nuclear physics research, and voltages of 15 million volts are practical.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.34 is the schematic of a research generator, the passage explains each part in terms of the chapter’s properties of conductors, and the problem on the field 5.00 m from a 3.00 mC terminal and the conceptual question in 18.7 on whether the belt can be a conductor apply them.

concepts.name: Xerography and the laser printer
concepts.why: Most copy machines use xerography, a dry copying process based on electrostatics. A selenium-coated aluminum drum is sprayed with positive charge from points; selenium is a photoconductor, an insulator in the dark and a conductor in the light, so where the image is light the charge leaks away to the grounded drum and where it is dark the positive charge remains. Negatively charged toner is attracted to the charged regions, a paper given a greater positive charge pulls the toner off the drum, and heated rollers melt it into the fibers. A laser printer makes the image on the drum with a scanned laser beam and is otherwise the same process.
concepts.evidence: Figures 18.35 and 18.36 draw the four stages and the laser printer, the passage names the photoconductor and the grounding of the drum, and the two glossary entries define the process and the printer.

concepts.name: Ink jet printers and electrostatic painting
concepts.why: An ink jet printer makes a fine spray of tiny ink droplets, gives them an electrostatic charge, and directs them with great precision using pairs of charged plates to form letters and images on paper, with a black jet and three colored jets producing color. Electrostatic painting charges paint the same way: mutual repulsion of like charges makes the paint fly from its source, surface tension forms drops, and the unlike charge of the surface draws them in, perpendicular to a conductor and with extra paint on corners and points.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.37 draws the nozzle, the charging electrodes and the deflection plates, and the passage under Ink Jet Printers and Electrostatic Painting explains both applications through the force on a charge in a field and the field of a conductor.

concepts.name: Electrostatic precipitators and air cleaning
concepts.why: An electrostatic air cleaner places excess charge, usually positive, on the smoke, dust, pollen and other particles in the air and then passes the air through an oppositely charged grid that attracts and retains them. Large precipitators remove over 99% of the particles from the stack gas of coal- and oil-fired plants, and home units remove polluting particles, irritants and allergens.
concepts.evidence: Figure 18.38 draws the schematic and shows a power plant with no visible smoke, the passage gives the process and the 99% figure, and 18.2’s problem on the speck of dust in a precipitator with a net charge of −5.00 nC is set in it.

concepts.name: The problem-solving strategy for electrostatics
concepts.why: Examine the situation to see whether static electricity is involved, identify the system with the number, locations and types of charges, list the unknowns and decide whether the Coulomb force is to be found directly, in which case a free-body diagram drawn with field lines helps, list the knowns, distinguishing the Coulomb force $F$ from the electric field $E$, solve the appropriate equation or draw the field lines, and examine the answer for reasonable size, sign and units. An unreasonable answer usually points to the premise that produced it, such as an excessively large separated charge.
concepts.evidence: The boxed Problem-Solving Strategies for Electrostatics and the boxed strategy for Unreasonable Results state the steps, 18.3’s and 18.4’s problems on the acceleration of two protons and of a proton in a field ask the reader to show the steps explicitly, and the three Unreasonable Results problems of the section ask which assumption is responsible.

concepts.name: Join electrostatics to Newton’s laws and kinematics
concepts.why: The electric field exerts a force on charges, and so the problems of electrostatics reach into dynamics, kinematics, circular motion, statics and fluids. The strategy is to identify the physical principles involved and the chapters they come from, then solve each part with that part’s own strategy: weight from $w = mg$, the electric force from $F = qE$, the acceleration from Newton’s second law with the net force, and the motion that follows from the kinematics of constant acceleration.
concepts.evidence: Example 18.5 finds the weight, the electric force and the upward acceleration of a charged drop of gasoline, and the Integrated Concepts problems of the section follow it: the electron orbiting a proton, the electron stopped by a field, the proton reaching 3.00% of the speed of light, the charged ball hanging at 8.00° in a field, the electron deflected between plates, the Millikan oil drop and the charge suspended above a square of charges.
